beats.narration_text: Ahoj — Liam, in for Bear. Episode 5 of 6. Today you attack your own engine, and then you chain it up. Two components, eighteen points. First, adversarial fragility: design one small, realistic perturbation — a distribution shift, a plausible data error, a gamed input — and find the conditions under which your engine flips its recommendation. The standard is blunt: a resource-moving tool that flips under a perturbation a human wouldn't notice is not understanding anything. Second, the delegation map and the hard-stop gate: for every component, what the tool decides, what you decide, and the named handoff where your judgment overrides the output — then the non-negotiable rule that the engine stops and asks a human before any move that spends money, commits a resource, or changes a person's access. Skip that gate without justification and it is minus fifteen, on top of whatever the missing points cost you. This is the episode where the tool learns its place. Let's break it.

beats.narration_text: The fragility test has a shape: small, realistic, and aimed at the decision — not the metric. Not 'accuracy dropped two points under noise.' The question is: under what perturbation does the MOVE change? Three families to pick from. Family one, distribution shift: replay your engine on the data as it looked one quarter earlier, or with the seasonality inverted. If the recommended move reverses across a boundary the model has no feature for, you have found the fragility. Family two, the plausible data error: one warehouse reports inventory in cases instead of units. One timestamp lands in the wrong timezone. A duplicate row from a retried upload. These are Tuesday-level errors — the kind your GIGO gate from episode 2 should catch, and now you get to test whether it actually does. Run the error through: does the gate stop it, or does the engine cheerfully reallocate on a typo? Family three, the gamed input — and for reallocation engines this is the sharpest one: the units being scored have an incentive to look needy or look deserving. A site that learns slightly inflating its demand forecast attracts more stock WILL inflate its demand forecast. Simulate the smallest gaming that captures the resource. Then document the flip condition precisely: this input, changed this much, flips the move from A-to-B to A-to-C. That number — how little it takes — is the finding.

lines: Aim at the decision, not the metric
Shift: replay last quarter / invert the seasonality
Plausible error: cases vs units , timezone slip , duplicate row

beats.narration_text: Now the delegation map. For every component of your system, three columns: what does the tool decide, what do you decide, and where exactly is the handoff — the point where your judgment overrides the output. Walk the pipeline. Data cleaning: the tool applies the gate; you decided what the gate is, and you personally review anything quarantined. Scoring: the tool computes; nobody overrides arithmetic. Ranking: the tool orders the options; you own the objective it ranks by — you wrote that sentence in episode 2, including what it leaves out. The recommendation: the tool proposes the move. The execution: stop. That line does not belong to the tool, and the map has to say so in writing. The named override point is not a platitude — it is a location. 'Human judgment matters' is not an override point. 'Before any transfer above two hundred units, the regional manager reviews the uncertainty interval, and if the interval includes zero benefit, the move does not execute' — that is an override point. Name whose judgment, at which step, empowered to do what. The map is also where you catch scope creep in your own build: if you find a component where the tool decides and no human is anywhere in the column, that is either a component that needs a human or a decision you have quietly abdicated. The map makes the abdication visible. That is its whole job.

lines: Tool decides , you decide , the named handoff
Cleaning: tool applies the gate — you wrote it, you review quarantine.
Scoring: tool computes. Nobody overrides arithmetic.

beats.narration_text: The hard stop. The rule is one sentence long: the engine may recommend a reallocation, but it must stop and require explicit human approval before executing any move that spends money, commits a resource, or changes a person's access. Implement it if it is in scope; if not, specify it precisely — but either way, name which of the three your engine would do, and why the gate is non-negotiable exactly there. The design has three parts. Part one, the trigger: which actions are gated. Be concrete — 'transfers over threshold T,' 'any change to an applicant's eligibility status,' 'any spend.' Part two, the response: when the gate trips, what happens — approve, flag, or block — and this is a policy you write per action class, not one global setting. Part three, the resolver: WHO approves. A name, a role, an accountability. 'A human reviews it' without a who is how review queues become rubber stamps. And understand why the assignment prices this at minus fifteen if absent: reallocation without a hard stop is how an accountable tool becomes an unaccountable one. 'It ran unattended and moved the budget' is not a bug report — it is the exact failure this entire course exists to prevent, reached one lazy default at a time. The gate is the difference between a tool that advises and a system that acts with nobody signing. Your engine advises. A person signs. Every time.

lines: Spends money , commits a resource , changes access / STOP
Trigger: which actions are gated — concrete thresholds, named action classes.

beats.narration_text: Verdict for Break It on Purpose and the Hard-Stop Gate. Fragility is tested at the decision, not the metric: one small, realistic perturbation — a shift, a Tuesday-level data error, a gamed forecast — and the documented condition under which the move flips. How little it takes is the finding, and whether your GIGO gate catches the error is the free second finding. The delegation map has three columns — tool decides, you decide, named handoff — and its job is to make abdication visible: any component with no human in the column is a decision you gave away without noticing. And the hard stop is non-negotiable wherever the engine would spend, commit, or change access: a concrete trigger, a per-class response — approve, flag, or block — and a named resolver who signs. The engine advises; a person signs. Final episode next: saying what the tool cannot know, the disclosure only you can write, and shipping the whole thing.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. The prompt to paste into Claude reads: Here is my engine's recommendation logic and its input schema: paste them. Design the smallest realistic perturbation — a plausible data error, a distribution shift, or a gamed input from a unit that wants the resource — that would flip my engine's recommended move. Then draft my delegation map: for each pipeline component, what the tool decides and what a human must decide. Mark every action that spends money, commits a resource, or changes a person's access, and propose a hard-stop policy for each: approve, flag, or block — and what information the approver needs on screen to decide well. Why run it: Claude is a genuinely good adversary — it will find gaming strategies you are too close to the build to see, and asking for the SMALLEST flip forces precision instead of catastrophizing. But notice the two fields it cannot fill. It can propose that someone approves the transfer; it cannot know that in your org, that someone is a shift supervisor with ninety seconds and no context — which is a rubber stamp, not a gate. And it cannot decide what the approver needs to see, because that is a claim about what a specific human can absorb under time pressure. Fill in the resolver and the review screen yourself. Those two decisions are the difference between a gate that exists and a gate that works.
